lines.text: What actually crosses a wire section when a lamp lights? Thinking in terms of moving particles makes current measurable.

An electric current is a flow of charge carriers. In a metal, free electrons move, in an electrolyte, positive and negative ions can move. A neutron has no charge, so a moving neutron alone does not carry electric current. Current describes charge flow, although the circuit can also transfer energy.
This idea lets us count the charge passing a section and then relate that count to time.
Electric current, flow of charge carriers. Metal, free electrons, electrolyte, ions. Uncharged particles alone carry no current.
Why can an ion beam carry current but a neutron beam cannot?
Oil droplets do not pick up arbitrary amounts of charge. Their measured charges occur in discrete steps.

Charge on a charge carrier is quantised, it is an integer multiple of the elementary charge e equals one point six zero times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs. Positive and negative multiples are possible, as is zero. Divide a proposed charge by e, the result must be an integer. For example, four point eight times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs equals three e is possible, whereas four point zero times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs equals two point five e is not.
The elementary charge also lets us convert between a number of electrons and total charge.
Carrier charge is an integer multiple of e. e equals one point six zero times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs. Test a proposed charge by dividing by e.
Why is minus three point two times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs possible but plus four point zero times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs impossible?
To compare charge flow in two circuits, count how much charge passes a section in the same time.

For a constant current, Q equals I t, charge Q in coulombs equals current I in amperes multiplied by time t in seconds. One coulomb is the charge transferred by one ampere in one second. Rearrange to I equals Q over t or t equals Q over I as required. If N carriers each have charge magnitude q, then Q equals N q, for electrons q equals e. In steady series flow, equal charge passes each section in the same time.
Combining Q equals I t with the number of carriers crossing a conductor leads to the drift relation.
Q equals I t for constant current. one coulomb passes with one ampere for one second. For N electrons, Q equals N e.
If a wire becomes narrower, why does the charge crossing each section in one second stay the same?
Electrons drift slowly through a wire, yet a measurable current flows because so many electrons cross each section.

For a current carrying conductor, I equals A n v q, where ay is cross sectional area, n is the number density of charge carriers, number per unit volume, v is average drift speed, and q is the magnitude of charge per carrier. In time t, carriers travel v t and sweep volume A v t. This contains n A v t carriers, whose charge magnitude is Q equals n A v t q. Since I equals Q over t, I equals A n v q. At fixed current in the same material, v is inversely proportional to ay.
The equation predicts that a narrow section has faster drift without any change in steady current.
n counts carriers per unit volume, in per cubic metre. Swept volume in time t is A v t. I equals A n v q, at fixed I, n, q, v is proportional to one over ay.

In one breath.
Electric current is a flow of charge carriers. Counting the charge that crosses a section gives Q equals I t, counting the carriers swept through a conductor gives I equals A n v q.
Key ideas.

An electric current is a flow of charge carriers. In a metal, free electrons carry charge through the conductor. In an electrolyte, moving positive and negative ions can carry charge. An energy transfer can accompany a current, but energy itself is not the charge carrier. Neutrons are uncharged, so their motion alone cannot make an electric current.

Conventional current points in the direction a positive charge would move, from the positive terminal towards the negative terminal through the external circuit. In a metal, the moving carriers are negative electrons, which drift towards the positive terminal, opposite to conventional current.

The charge on a carrier is quantised, it is an integer multiple of the elementary charge, e equals one point six zero times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs. A carrier can have plus e, minus e, plus two e, minus three e, and so on, zero is also an integer multiple. Check a proposed charge by dividing it by e. For example, four point eight times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs equals three e is possible, but four point zero times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs equals two point five e is not. The sign tells you the type of charge and does not invalidate a value.

Current measures the rate at which charge crosses a fixed section. For constant current, Q equals I t, where Q is charge in coulombs, I is current in amperes and t is time in seconds. Thus one coulomb is the charge transferred by a current of one ampere in one second. If Q is known, I equals Q over t, if a count N of electrons is known, use the charge magnitude Q equals N e.

For a current carrying conductor, I equals A n v q. Here ay is cross sectional area in square metres, n is the number density of charge carriers in per cubic metre, number per unit volume, v is their average drift speed in metres per second, and q is the magnitude of charge per carrier in coulombs. This equation gives the magnitude of current, electron drift is opposite to conventional current. In time t, carriers travel v t and sweep out volume A v t. The number of carriers in that volume is n A v t, so Q equals n A v t q. Dividing by t yields I equals A n v q.
Method.
Identify the section that charge crosses and whether the question gives a total charge, a carrier count, or a number density.
Convert time to seconds, area to square metres and any wire length to metres. A circular wire has ay equals pi d squared over four, doubling diameter makes area four times larger.

Use Q equals I t for total charge or I equals A n v q for drift. If the total carrier count N in a length L is given, n equals N over open bracket ay L close bracket, so I equals N q v over L, the unknown area cancels.
Check that your answer has the expected unit and sensible magnitude. At fixed current in the same material, n and q are fixed, so drift speed is inversely proportional to area.
Worked example.

Calculate its current. State the equation, I equals A n v q, with q equals e. is greater than I equals open bracket two point zero times ten to the minus six close bracket open bracket eight point zero times ten to the twenty eight close bracket open bracket one point zero times ten to the minus four close bracket open bracket one point six zero times ten to the minus nineteen close bracket equals two point five six amperes point is greater than. To two significant figures, I equals two point six amperes. The electron drift direction does not make the current magnitude negative.

Their average drift speed is v equals two point zero times ten to the minus five metres per second. Calculate the current magnitude without knowing the cross sectional area. Convert the length, L equals twenty centimetres equals zero point two zero metres. The wire volume is ay L, so n equals N over open bracket ay L close bracket. Substitute into I equals A n v q, using the electron charge magnitude q equals e, is greater than I equals A open bracket N over ay L close bracket v e equals N e v over L point is greater than. The area cancels, divide by length because N is the count in the whole wire, not the count per unit length. is greater than I equals open bracket three point zero times ten to the twenty two close bracket open bracket one point six zero times ten to the minus nineteen close bracket open bracket two point zero times ten to the minus five close bracket, all over zero point two zero equals zero point four eight amperes point is greater than. Check, for fixed N, ay and v, a larger L means a larger volume and a smaller number density, so the current decreases. Doubling L halves n and I.

Traps.
Trap, Calling n carriers per unit area. Why it's wrong, n A alone has units of carriers per metre. Instead, Use carriers per unit volume, multiply by the swept volume A v t.
Trap, Assuming twice the diameter means twice the area. Why it's wrong, Area depends on diameter squared. Instead, Square the diameter ratio before comparing drift speeds.

Trap, Changing charge passing each section of a steady wire according to its width. Why it's wrong, Current is the same through consecutive sections. Instead, For equal time intervals, Q equals I t gives equal charge, while drift speed adjusts.
Exam technique.

For State or Define, use flow of charge carriers and number per unit volume precisely. For Calculate, write the equation, substitute in S I units and give the unit. For Show that I equals A n v q, explicitly write the swept volume, carrier count and charge before dividing by time. When testing quantisation, display the ratio to e and check that it is an integer.
